report.title: Comparing SQLite and PostgreSQL for Small Web Applications
report.summary: Choosing between SQLite and PostgreSQL for a small web app depends primarily on your concurrency needs and your tolerance for operational overhead. SQLite is an embedded library stored in a single file that requires zero configuration, making it exceptionally easy to deploy [E6][E11]. PostgreSQL is a traditional client-server database that offers robust performance for complex, high-concurrency workloads [E1][E11].

sections.heading: Concurrency and Performance
sections.content:
PostgreSQL excels in environments requiring heavy write concurrency. It uses true Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) to support many concurrent writers without blocking readers, and it handles larger datasets and intricate queries effectively [E1][E11].

SQLite operates as an embedded library with in-process calls that achieve microsecond read latencies [E11]. While Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) allows concurrent reads, SQLite limits write concurrency to a single writer at a time [E11]. For a small web app with modest write volumes, this performance is often more than sufficient.

sections.heading: Hosting and Operational Complexity
sections.content:
SQLite eliminates an entire class of operational work. Because the database is just a file, it requires no separate server process, network port configuration, user management, or database administrator [E6][E11]. While traditional deployments relied solely on local files, modern tools like Litestream enable straightforward backups to cloud storage [E8][E9].

PostgreSQL runs as a dedicated database daemon that requires active server installation and ongoing maintenance [E11]. Administrators must manage roles, tune configuration files, and monitor parameters like autovacuum and WAL [E11]. If your small web app aims to minimize infrastructure management, SQLite offers a compelling advantage [E12].

### Performance and Concurrency
- **SQLite:** Operates as an embedded library with microsecond read latencies due to in-process calls [E11]. It allows concurrent reads via WAL (Write-Ahead Logging), but write concurrency is limited to a single writer at a time [E11].
- **PostgreSQL:** Uses a client-server architecture with true MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control), supporting many concurrent writers without blocking readers [E11]. It handles larger datasets, complex queries, and high write concurrency much better [E1].

### Hosting and Operational Complexity
- **SQLite:** Features zero configuration where the database is stored in a single file, requiring no separate server process, database administrator, user management, or network port configuration [E6][E11]. Modern extensions like Litestream or LiteFS enable backups and replication [E8][E9].
- **PostgreSQL:** Runs as a dedicated database daemon requiring server installation, configuration tuning, role management, and ongoing maintenance of parameters like WAL and autovacuum [E11].

# Comparing SQLite and PostgreSQL for Small Web Applications

Choosing between SQLite and PostgreSQL for a small web app depends primarily on your concurrency needs and your tolerance for operational overhead. SQLite is an embedded library stored in a single file that requires zero configuration, making it exceptionally easy to deploy [E6][E11]. PostgreSQL is a traditional client-server database that offers robust performance for complex, high-concurrency workloads [E1][E11].

## Concurrency and Performance

PostgreSQL excels in environments requiring heavy write concurrency. It uses true Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) to support many concurrent writers without blocking readers, and it handles larger datasets and intricate queries effectively [E1][E11]. 

SQLite operates as an embedded library with in-process calls that achieve microsecond read latencies [E11]. While Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) allows concurrent reads, SQLite limits write concurrency to a single writer at a time [E11]. For a small web app with modest write volumes, this performance is often more than sufficient.

## Hosting and Operational Complexity

SQLite eliminates an entire class of operational work. Because the database is just a file, it requires no separate server process, network port configuration, user management, or database administrator [E6][E11]. While traditional deployments relied solely on local files, modern tools like Litestream enable straightforward backups to cloud storage [E8][E9]. 

PostgreSQL runs as a dedicated database daemon that requires active server installation and ongoing maintenance [E11]. Administrators must manage roles, tune configuration files, and monitor parameters like autovacuum and WAL [E11]. If your small web app aims to minimize infrastructure management, SQLite offers a compelling advantage [E12].
